# Book I, Proposition 20

*Two sides exceed the third*

> In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/20-idea.svg" alt="Lay any two sides of a triangle end to end (blue and yellow), and together they are longer than the third side (red)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Lay any two sides of a triangle end to end (blue and yellow), and together they are longer than the third side (red).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/20.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.20, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For let ABC be a triangle;

I say that in the triangle ABC two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one, namely

BA, AC greater than BC,

AB, BC greater than AC,

BC, CA greater than AB.

For let BA be drawn through to the point D,

let DA be made equal to CA, and let DC be joined.

Then, since DA is equal to AC,

the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]

therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]

And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,

and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]

therefore DB is greater than BC.

But DA is equal to AC;

therefore BA, AC are greater than BC.

Similarly we can prove that AB, BC are also greater than CA, and BC, CA than AB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

```lean
/-! ## What Euclid reads off the figure -/

/-- Room to cut off `AD`. "Let BA be drawn through to the point D, let DA be made
equal to CA": that is I.3's work, and I.3 cuts off from a *greater* straight line,
while Postulate 2 produces `BA` without saying how far. So first produce `BA` beyond
`A` further than `AC`: describe the circle with centre `A` and distance `AC`
(Post. 3), take `Y` where `BA` produced beyond the centre cuts it (System E,
Intersections 5), and produce `AY` a little further still, to `X` (Post. 2). Then
`AX` is greater than `AY`, which is equal to `AC` [Def. 15]. -/
theorem Prop20.produced {A B C : Point} (hBA : B ≠ A) (hAC : A ≠ C) :
    ∃ X : Point, Between B A X ∧ ‖A C‖ < ‖A X‖ := by
  obtain ⟨α, hA_α, hC_α⟩ := Postulate3 A C hAC
  obtain ⟨L, hB_L, hA_L⟩ := Postulate1 B A hBA
  obtain ⟨Y, hY_α, -, hYAB⟩ := line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hA_α) hA_L hB_L hBA
  obtain ⟨X, hAYX⟩ := produce (ne_of_between hYAB).symm
  refine ⟨X, between_of_between_right (between_symm hYAB) hAYX, ?_⟩
  rw [Definition15 hA_α hC_α hY_α]
  exact len_lt_of_between hAYX

/-- What Euclid sees in his figure: `CA` falls within the angle `BCD`, because `A`
lies between `B` and `D`; so the angle `BCD` is made up of the angles `BCA` and
`ACD` (`angle_add_of_between`), and `BCA` is something, since `B` is off the
straight line `CA` (System E, Diagram-angle 1). The whole is greater than the
part. -/
theorem Prop20.part {A B C D : Point} (hBDC : Triangle B D C) (hBAD : Between B A D) :
    ∠ A C D < ∠ B C D := by
  have hBCD : ∠ B C D = ∠ B C A + ∠ A C D := angle_add_of_between hBDC hBAD
  obtain ⟨L, hB_L, hD_L⟩ := Postulate1 B D hBDC.ne₁₂
  have hA_L : OnLine A L := on_line_of_between_ends hBAD hB_L hD_L
  have hC_L : ¬ OnLine C L := hBDC.off_line hB_L hD_L
  have hC_A : C ≠ A := fun e => hC_L (e ▸ hA_L)
  have hB_A : B ≠ A := ne_of_between hBAD
  have hB_C : B ≠ C := fun e => hC_L (e ▸ hB_L)
  obtain ⟨M, hC_M, hA_M⟩ := Postulate1 C A hC_A
  have hB_M : ¬ OnLine B M := fun hB_M =>
    hC_L ((line_unique hB_A hB_M hA_M hB_L hA_L) ▸ hC_M)
  have hBCA : 0 < ∠ B C A := Magnitude.pos_of_ne_zero fun h0 => by
    rw [angle_symm hB_C hC_A.symm] at h0
    exact hB_M (same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero hC_A hB_C.symm hC_M hA_M h0).1
  rw [hBCD, add_comm]
  exact CommonNotion5 hBCA

/-- In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one. -/
theorem Prop20 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) :
    ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ ∧ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ ∧ ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖ := by
  -- For let ABC be a triangle;
  -- I say that in the triangle ABC two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the
  -- remaining one, namely
  -- BA, AC greater than BC,
  -- AB, BC greater than AC,
  -- BC, CA greater than AB.
  /- Euclid proves the first, and says "similarly" for the other two. So we give his
     argument for every triangle, in his letters, and use it three times below. -/
  have greater : ∀ {A B C : Point}, Triangle A B C → ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
    intro A B C hABC
    have hB_A : B ≠ A := hABC.ne₁₂.symm
    have hA_C : A ≠ C := hABC.ne₁₃
    obtain ⟨BA, hB_BA, hA_BA⟩ := Postulate1 B A hB_A
    have hC_BA : ¬ OnLine C BA := hABC.bac.off_line hB_BA hA_BA
    -- For let BA be drawn through to the point D,
    /- Drawn through beyond A to a point X, far enough for I.3 to cut AD off from AX:
       `Prop20.produced`. -/
    obtain ⟨X, hBAX, hAC_AX⟩ := Prop20.produced hB_A hA_C
    -- let DA be made equal to CA, and let DC be joined.
    /- Heath gives no bracket here, but "let DA be made equal" is I.3's work, as in
       I.11 and I.16: cut off AD from AX. Then D lies between A and X, and so A lies
       between B and D: BA drawn through reaches D. -/
    obtain ⟨D, hADX, hAD_CA⟩ := Prop3 (A := A) (B := X) hA_C.symm
      (by rw [len_symm C A]; exact hAC_AX)
    have hBAD : Between B A D :=
      between_symm (between_inner (between_symm hADX) (between_symm hBAX))
    have hD_BA : OnLine D BA := on_line_of_between hBAD hB_BA hA_BA
    have hA_D : A ≠ D := ne_of_between hADX
    have hD_C : D ≠ C := fun e => hC_BA (e ▸ hD_BA)
    obtain ⟨DC, hD_DC, hC_DC⟩ := Postulate1 D C hD_C
    -- Then, since DA is equal to AC,
    have hDA_AC : ‖D A‖ = ‖A C‖ := by rw [len_symm D A, hAD_CA, len_symm C A]
    -- the angle ADC is also equal to the angle ACD; [I. 5]
    /- I.5 for the triangle ADC, whose sides AD, AC are equal. Its statement also
       speaks of the equal sides produced, so Lean produces them (Post. 2), though
       only the angles at the base are wanted here. -/
    have hADC : Triangle A D C := Triangle.of_line hA_BA hD_BA hA_D hC_BA
    obtain ⟨P, hADP⟩ := produce hA_D
    obtain ⟨Q, hACQ⟩ := produce hA_C
    have hADC_ACD : ∠ A D C = ∠ A C D :=
      (Prop5 hADC (by rw [← len_symm D A]; exact hDA_AC) hADP hACQ).1
    -- therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC. [C.N. 5]
    /- Greater than the angle ACD, which is equal to it: CA falls within the angle
       BCD, since A lies between B and D, and the whole is greater than the part
       (`Prop20.part`). -/
    have hBDC : Triangle B D C :=
      Triangle.of_line hB_BA hD_BA (ne_of_between_ends hBAD) hC_BA
    have hADC_BCD : ∠ A D C < ∠ B C D := by
      rw [hADC_ACD]
      exact Prop20.part hBDC hBAD
    -- And, since DCB is a triangle having the angle BCD greater than the angle BDC,
    /- The angle BDC is the angle ADC, since A lies on the ray from D through B
       (`angle_onRay_left`). -/
    have hDCB : Triangle D C B := hBDC.bca
    have hBDC_BCD : ∠ B D C < ∠ B C D := by
      rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hBAD)) hD_C.symm]
      exact hADC_BCD
    -- and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]
    /- I.19 for the triangle BCD, named from B: the angle at C is greater than the
       angle at D, so the side BD, opposite C, is greater than the side BC, opposite
       D. -/
    have hBC_BD : ‖B C‖ < ‖B D‖ :=
      Prop19 hDCB.cba (by rw [angle_symm hD_C.symm (ne_of_between_ends hBAD)]; exact hBDC_BCD)
    -- therefore DB is greater than BC.
    have hBC_DB : ‖B C‖ < ‖D B‖ := by rw [len_symm D B]; exact hBC_BD
    -- But DA is equal to AC;
    /- And DB is BA and AD together, since A lies between B and D (System E,
       Diagram-segment 1); so DB is BA and AC together. -/
    have hDB : ‖D B‖ = ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := by
      rw [← hDA_AC, len_symm D A, len_add_of_between hBAD, len_symm D B]
    -- therefore BA, AC are greater than BC.
    rw [← hDB]
    exact hBC_DB
  /- Euclid's argument, in his own figure: BA, AC are greater than BC. -/
  have hBC : ‖B C‖ < ‖B A‖ + ‖A C‖ := greater hABC
  -- Similarly we can prove that AB, BC are also greater than CA, and BC, CA than AB.
  /- The same argument for the triangle BAC, with AB drawn through beyond B, and for
     the triangle CBA, with BC drawn through beyond C. -/
  have hAC : ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ + ‖B C‖ := greater hABC.bac
  have hAB : ‖A B‖ < ‖B C‖ + ‖C A‖ := by
    rw [len_symm A B]
    exact greater hABC.cba
  -- Therefore etc.
  exact ⟨hBC, hAC, hAB⟩
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**Evident even to an ass.** Heath tells the story: "It was the habit of the Epicureans, says Proclus (p. 323), to ridicule this theorem as being evident even to an ass and requiring no proof, and their allegation that the theorem was 'known' (γνώριμον) even to an ass was based on the fact that, if fodder is placed at one angular point and the ass at another, he does not, in order to get to his food, traverse the two sides of the triangle but only the one side separating them." It is "an argument which makes Savile exclaim that its authors were 'digni ipsi, qui cum Asino foenum essent'": fit to eat hay with the ass themselves. "Proclus replies truly that a mere perception of the truth of the theorem is a different thing from a scientific proof of it and a knowledge of the reason why it is true. Moreover, as Simson says, the number of axioms should not be increased without necessity" (vol. 1, p. 287). Lean takes Simson's side. Neither our tacit rules nor System E's, from which they come, say that two sides of a triangle are greater than the third, so I.20 has to be proved, and it is proved here from I.5 and I.19, as Euclid does it.

**Room to cut off AD.** "Let BA be drawn through to the point D, let DA be made equal to CA." Heath gives no bracket, but making one straight line equal to another on a straight line produced is the work of I.3, as in I.11 and I.16, and I.3 cuts off only from a *greater* straight line. [`Prop20.produced`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop20.lean) makes room. Describe the circle with centre A and distance AC (Post. 3). BA, produced beyond the centre, cuts it at some point (System E, Intersections 5), and produced a little further still (Post. 2) it is greater than AC [Def. 15]. Then I.3 cuts AD off it, and one fact of order from Book Zero, `between_inner`, puts A between B and D. It is the step that `Prop11.produced` and `Prop16.beyond` take, said once for any length laid off from A. As in I.11, the circle has already marked a point at the right distance, so Lean could do without I.3, but "made equal" is I.3's step, and we take it.

**What Lean made us say.** "Therefore the angle BCD is greater than the angle ADC [C.N. 5]": greater, that is, than the angle ACD, which I.5 has just made equal to ADC. The whole is greater than the part only if CA falls within the angle BCD, and it does because A lies between B and D. [`Prop20.part`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop20.lean) says so: the angle BCD is made up of BCA and ACD (`angle_add_of_between`, from Pasch 2 and Diagram-angle 2), and BCA is something, since B is off the straight line CA (Diagram-angle 1). In the next breath Euclid speaks of the angle BDC where he had ADC, and they are one angle because A lies on the ray from D through B (`angle_onRay_left`). I.19 is then applied to the triangle DCB, which is a triangle because C is off the straight line BD (`Triangle.of_line`). And "But DA is equal to AC; therefore BA, AC are greater than BC" rests on DB being BA and AD together, since A lies between B and D (System E, Diagram-segment 1). Each of these rules is Jeremy Avigad, Edward Dean and John Mumma's, and LeanEuclid's careful Lean version of System E, by Logan Murphy, Kaiyu Yang, Jialiang Sun, Zhaoyu Li, Anima Anandkumar and Xujie Si, was open beside us the whole way.

**I.5, with its sides produced.** Our I.5 states both of its parts, the angles at the base and the angles under it, so to cite it Lean must produce AD and AC beyond D and C (Book Zero's `produce`), though only the angles at the base are wanted here. I.7 does the same.

**"Similarly."** Euclid proves that BA, AC are greater than BC, and leaves the other two pairs to the reader. As in I.16, the Lean gives his argument once, for every triangle, and uses it three times: in the triangle ABC as Euclid draws it, in BAC with AB drawn through beyond B, and in CBA with BC drawn through beyond C. Naming a triangle from another corner (`Triangle.bac`, `Triangle.cba`) and reading a straight line from either end (`len_symm`) are all the "similarly" needs.

**Heron and Porphyry.** They proved the theorem, Heath reports from Proclus, "without producing one of the sides" (vol. 1, p. 287). In the first proof the angle BAC is bisected by AD meeting BC in D; by I.16 the exterior angle ADC is greater than the angle BAD, "that is, greater than the angle DAC", so by I.19 "the side AC is greater than the side CD"; similarly AB is greater than BD, and the two are added. In Lean, AD meeting BC would be I.9 together with Book Zero's `crossbar`. The second, also direct, has to sort the triangles into cases, and the third is by *reductio ad absurdum* (vol. 1, pp. 287–288). Euclid's own needs only one figure.

**The modern way.** For vectors u and v, |u + v|² = |u|² + 2u·v + |v|², and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality u·v ≤ |u||v| makes this at most (|u| + |v|)², with equality only when u and v point the same way, that is, when the triangle has collapsed onto a straight line. In the complex plane it reads |z + w| ≤ |z| + |w|; and what Euclid proves, the modern theory of metric spaces takes as part of the definition of distance, under the name of the triangle inequality.
